subject: geography
title: El Niño, La Niña and Ocean Circulation
welcome_lead: From the Humboldt Current to global rainfall, study how Pacific oscillations ripple across the planet.
meta_desc: IBDP Geography Adventure: El Niño-Southern Oscillation, ocean circulation and global teleconnections.
final_note: You have ridden the ENSO see-saw. Oceans and atmosphere are coupled, with global consequences.

concepts.def: El Niño-Southern Oscillation: coupled ocean-atmosphere mode of variability in the tropical Pacific.
Warm phase of ENSO with weakened trade winds and warmer eastern Pacific.
Cool phase of ENSO with strengthened trade winds and cooler eastern Pacific.
Global ocean conveyor belt driven by temperature and salinity gradients.
Vertical movement of cold, nutrient-rich water to the surface supporting major fisheries.
Linkage of weather patterns across great distances, e.g. ENSO effects on Indian monsoon.

walkthroughs.body_html: In neutral conditions, trade winds push warm surface water westward across the Pacific, supporting the Western Pacific Warm Pool and allowing cool upwelling along the South American coast — the productive Humboldt Current.

In an El Niño event, trade winds weaken or reverse. Warm water sloshes east, suppressing upwelling off Peru and devastating anchovy fisheries. Rainfall shifts: floods in Peru and Ecuador, droughts in Indonesia, Australia and southern Africa. The 1997-98 and 2015-16 events were especially severe.

La Niña intensifies trade winds, cooling the eastern Pacific. Australia and Indonesia tend to be wetter, while the south-western United States suffers drought. Atlantic hurricane activity often increases. The thermohaline circulation operates alongside ENSO; its potential slowdown is a major climate concern.
